newsitem.title: USA: Fed exhibit lets visitors play at central banking.
newsitem.headline: Fed exhibit lets visitors play at central banking.

text.p: Do you have an uncontrollable desire to safeguard the U.S. banking system, stabilize the currency or save the country from the ravages of inflation?
If so, then step right up to the intriguing and accessible interactive games and displays at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's new permanent exhibit "FedWorks."
The exhibit is one manifestation of Fed Bank of New York President William McDonough's long articulated commitment to educating the public about the purpose of central banking.

"The bank is increasingly involved in educational programs and President McDonough has a long-running interest in seeing that the public understand this institution," said Fed public information officer Steve Malin.
"The idea is both to demystify the Fed and to debunk the myths," he said.

Open to tour groups by appointment, the exhibit is expected to attract about 25,000 visitors a year. And if the New York Fed's popular gold vault tour is any indication, about two-thirds of those visitors will come with school groups, Malin said.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York, at 33 Liberty Street in Manhattan's financial district, has a fortress-like appearance. Its massive walls are bulwarks of giant stones. Ironwork by Samuel Yellin marks the entrance, behind which guards, polite but armed, stand alert.
To dispel some of that severity, the opening display in the exhibit is a hologram of a gold bar. But wait. Is it real or it is "Memorex?"
It turns out that when you try to grasp that gold, there's no there there. It's intriguing. It's amazing. Or as visiting high school students might put it, "It's cool."
The hologram was created for the New York Fed by the New York firm of DMA Inc, Malin said.
The rest of the exhibit is more substantial but equally engaging.
First is a 20-minute video presentation, intended to be watched for a few minutes and to encourage the viewer to move on to see the rest of the exhibit.
Displays of shredded money, currency renderings and counterfeit bills catch the eye.
An appealing graphic of a tree illustrates the Federal Reserve and all its branches -- a central bank that, in a real way, is decentralized, said Malin.
Another graphic outlines the historic development of the central bank from the early days of the republic to the present.
The Fed wears many hats, according to one vivid display illustrating the central bank's varied functions.

Like a football quarterback, the Fed's domestic open market desk of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York executes strategy -- the monetary policy strategy set by the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
Like a firefighter, the Fed helps to contain and extinguish financial crises before they spread by promoting financial and economic stability and public confidence.
And like a detective, the Fed examines the currency it processes in order to detect counterfeiting.
The visitor to "FedWorks" can pretend to work at the Fed's open market desk, adding or draining reserves from the banking system, adjusting to changing needs for credit.
If you have a secret yen to deliberate with the FOMC, first look at the 12 ingredients of the Fed's economic analysis.

Just like a Fed governor or a Fed bank president, you can evaluate factors -- like real Gross Domestic Product, retail sales, employment, durable goods orders, housing starts, industrial production, consumer prices, M2 money supply, business inventories, the 30-year bond yield, the S&P 500, and vehicle sales -- that the Fed considers key to evaluating the economy and to making monetary policy adjustments.
When you have studied all this, you can play one of the exhibit's interactive games on making policy.

In a game called, "Can You Keep the Economy on a Stable Course?", you can choose to raise or lower interest rates or to maintain rates where they are, depending on which scenario of growth, unemployment and inflation the game presents.
This reporter did well with the scenarios the game offered -- but she's still hanging on to her day job.
